claim: Only `name` and `description` are required in a subagent file's YAML frontmatter.
why: Tools, model, and permission mode have documented defaults when their fields are omitted.
check: Flag a missing `name` or `description` in a file intended to define a subagent.
quote: Only `name` and `description` are required.

claim: Multi-word subagent frontmatter keys use camelCase, and Claude Code ignores unrecognized fields without reporting them in the session.
why: A misspelled key leaves its intended setting unapplied, though `--debug` can identify unrecognized keys on supported versions.
check: Compare top-level keys with the frontmatter reference, especially when a configured restriction appears to have no effect.
quote: Claude Code ignores a field it doesn't recognize without reporting an error.

claim: Subagent frontmatter supports optional settings for tools, model, permissions, context, and execution in addition to the required `name` and `description`.
why: The value also accepts `description`, `tools`, `disallowedTools`, `model`, `permissionMode`, `mcpServers`, `hooks`, `maxTurns`, `autoCompactWindow`, `skills`, `initialPrompt`, `memory`, `effort`, `background`, `omitClaudeMd`, and `isolation`.
check: Compare optional keys with the frontmatter reference, and use `prompt` in `--agents` JSON for the system prompt that Markdown files put in the body.
quote: `description`, `tools`, `disallowedTools`, `model`, `permissionMode`, `mcpServers`, `hooks`, `maxTurns`, `autoCompactWindow`, `skills`, `initialPrompt`, `memory`, `effort`, `background`, `omitClaudeMd`, and `isolation`.

claim: If a subagent omits `tools` it inherits every tool available to subagents, including MCP tools.
why: The inherited pool can include write-capable tools, and an explicit `tools` allowlist or `disallowedTools` denylist can narrow it.
check: For a role intended to be read-only, inspect whether its effective tool pool includes write-capable tools.
quote: Inherits every tool available to subagents if omitted.

claim: When both `tools` and `disallowedTools` are set, the denylist is applied first, then the allowlist is resolved against what remains, and a tool in both is removed.
why: This order determines the final tool set when the two fields overlap.
check: Check overlapping entries when an agent is expected to use a tool listed in both fields, and check for an empty resolved allowlist if the agent fails to launch.
quote: If both are set, `disallowedTools` is applied first, then `tools` is resolved against the remaining pool. A tool listed in both is removed.

claim: A `disallowedTools` entry with a specifier such as `Bash(git push *)` removes the whole Bash tool from the subagent, not only the matching commands.
why: To block specific commands while keeping Bash, the docs say to use a Bash deny rule in `permissions.deny`, which applies to the main conversation and subagents.
check: Flag `disallowedTools: Bash(...)` entries that were meant as command-level filters; they disable Bash entirely.
quote: A `disallowedTools` entry with a specifier, such as `Bash(git push *)`, still removes the whole tool from the subagent, not only the matching commands.

claim: For custom subagents, the default model order is the invocation's `model`, the definition's `model` (including `inherit`), `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL`, then the spawning conversation's model.
why: Any `availableModels` allowlist can cause Claude Code to substitute a model when the selected value is blocked.
check: Trace an unexpected model through the invocation, definition, environment, parent, and any `availableModels` allowlist, then confirm the running model in `/tasks`.
quote:
When more than one source sets a model, Claude Code uses the first in this order:

1. The per-invocation `model` parameter, which Claude can pass when it starts the subagent. On an Agent tool call, the parameter takes a model alias, not a full model ID or `inherit`.
2. The `model` field in the subagent's definition, including `inherit`

claim: To route exploration to a lower-cost model, Anthropic suggests defining a user or project agent named `Explore` with `model: haiku` to override built-in Explore.
why: A user or project `Explore` keeps its own model field, which lets you route this role to a lower-cost model.
check: When exploration is intentionally routed to a lower-cost model, check that the override is named `Explore` and has the intended `model`.
quote: so define one with `model: haiku` to run exploration on a lower-cost model.

claim: Built-in Explore, Plan, and `web-fetch` skip startup CLAUDE.md, and Explore and Plan also skip git status.
why: Skipping startup context keeps research fast and inexpensive, and `omitClaudeMd` lets a custom subagent skip instructions independently of git status.
check: Check whether a built-in agent is expected to receive project instructions at startup and whether a custom agent's instructions or git snapshot load under its settings.
quote: Explore and Plan start without your CLAUDE.md files and the git status snapshot to keep research fast and inexpensive.

claim: When the combined `description` fields of non-built-in subagents exceed 15,000 tokens, Claude Code warns at startup but still loads every subagent.
why: Subagent descriptions consume context, so the docs advise keeping them short and moving detail into the system prompt that loads when the agent runs.
check: Check the combined token count in the startup warning and move detailed instructions out of oversized descriptions.
quote: Keep descriptions brief: Claude Code shows a startup warning when your subagents' combined descriptions pass [the 15,000-token limit](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/errors.md#agent-descriptions-are-over-the-15000-token-limit), and still loads every subagent.

claim: A non-fork subagent starts with fresh context and receives a delegation message without inheriting conversation history, already invoked skills, or files the main session has read.
why: The delegation message carries the task into the fresh context, which can also contain startup inputs such as project instructions.
check: Check for handoffs that rely on prior conversation, invoked skills, or earlier file reads without passing the needed information.
quote: Each subagent starts with a fresh, isolated context window. It doesn't see your conversation history, the skills you've already invoked, or the files Claude has already read.

claim: A non-fork subagent starts with its own system prompt, the delegation message, and any instruction files, git snapshot, and preloaded skills that apply to that agent.
why: Explore, Plan, and `web-fetch` skip initial instruction files, Explore and Plan skip git status, and other startup inputs depend on `omitClaudeMd`, `includeGitInstructions`, and the agent's `skills` list.
check: Check whether the subagent is actually configured to load any CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, git status, or preloaded skill content that its prompt assumes.
quote:
A non-fork subagent's initial context contains:

* **System prompt**: the agent's own prompt plus environment details that Claude Code appends, not the Claude Code system prompt.

claim: A non-fork subagent uses its own model's context window and receives neither the main session's output style nor its auto memory.
why: The subagent runs its own system prompt, and its `memory` field enables separate persistent auto memory.
check: Do not credit a setup for output-style rules reaching subagents; check that long-input subagents are on a model with an adequate window.
quote: **Output style**: a subagent runs its own system prompt, so your

claim: A custom non-fork subagent uses its own system prompt with basic environment details in place of the default Claude Code system prompt.
why: The Markdown body or JSON `prompt` supplies that system prompt, and headless callers can append to it with the documented flags.
check: Check for behavior the setup expects from the default Claude Code system prompt even though the custom subagent supplies its own.
quote: Subagents receive this system prompt plus basic environment details like the working directory, not the Claude Code system prompt.

claim: `omitClaudeMd: true` skips user, project, and local CLAUDE.md at subagent startup, while managed policy files still load unless the subagent is managed.
why: The option is intended for self-contained delegation, and it is ignored when the agent runs as the main session via `--agent` or the `agent` setting.
check: Check whether an affected subagent still receives conventions it needs, including through the handoff or rules that load when it works in a subdirectory.
quote: Use it for subagents that take everything they need from the delegation prompt.

claim: The `skills` field preloads full skill content for the first 32 distinct names without restricting which other skills the subagent can invoke through `Skill`.
why: To prevent skill invocation, deny `Skill` or leave it out of an explicit `tools` allowlist.
check: Check whether a required preload falls after the first 32 distinct names or whether the setup mistakes preloading for a skill allowlist.
quote: The full content of each listed skill is injected into the subagent's context at startup, up to the first 32 distinct names in the list. This field controls which skills are preloaded, not which skills the subagent can access: without it, the subagent can still discover and invoke project, user, and plugin skills through the Skill tool during execution.

claim: Skills that set `disable-model-invocation: true` cannot be preloaded into a subagent through `skills`.
why: Preloading draws from the same set of skills Claude can invoke.
check: Flag a `skills:` list naming a manual-only skill; it will be skipped.
quote: since preloading draws from the same set of skills Claude can invoke.

claim: Plugin-supplied subagents ignore the `hooks`, `mcpServers` and `permissionMode` frontmatter fields.
why: Security: the docs say to copy the file into `.claude/agents/` or `~/.claude/agents/` if those fields are needed.
check: Flag plugin agents relying on those fields for safety restrictions; they are not enforced.
quote: For security reasons, plugin subagents don't support the `hooks`, `mcpServers`, or `permissionMode` frontmatter fields.

claim: Subagents inherit an unset `permissionMode` from the main session, which also overrides explicit subagent modes when it runs in bypassPermissions, acceptEdits, or auto.
why: A plan-mode main session also keeps subagents in plan mode, except when they run under agent-team rules, and a subagent set to `dontAsk` still suppresses prompts.
check: If a role relies on `permissionMode: plan` or `default`, check whether the actual main-session mode overrides it.
quote: When the main conversation is in `bypassPermissions`, `acceptEdits`, or [auto mode](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes.md#eliminate-prompts-with-auto-mode), your subagent runs in that same mode and Claude Code ignores the `permissionMode` you set.

claim: With auto memory and subagent `memory` enabled, Claude Code enables Read, Write, and Edit and includes up to the first 200 lines or 25KB of `MEMORY.md`, whichever comes first.
why: Memory enables those tools for managing memory files, and the recommended default scope is `project` because it can be shared via version control.
check: Check for read-only roles that enable subagent memory and may therefore receive Write and Edit.
quote:
The subagent's system prompt also includes the first 200 lines or 25KB of `MEMORY.md` in the memory directory, whichever comes first, with instructions to curate `MEMORY.md` if it exceeds that limit.
* Read, Write, and Edit tools are automatically enabled so the subagent can manage its memory files.

claim: `maxTurns` caps a subagent's agentic turns, and on Claude Code v2.1.246 or later the output is marked partial when the cap is reached.
why: Claude can resume the subagent to continue after it stops at the limit.
check: Check whether downstream steps treat partial output from a turn-limited subagent as complete.
quote: When the subagent reaches the limit, Claude Code returns its output marked as partial, and Claude can [resume it](#resume-subagents) to continue. The partial marking requires Claude Code v2.1.246 or later

claim: A subagent Claude spawns from the main conversation starts in the background by default, except for built-in `web-fetch`, and `background: true` keeps a subagent there even when Claude asks to wait.
why: Background results reach Claude as a completion notification in a later turn, while a foreground subagent blocks the main conversation until it finishes.
check: For work that needs an immediate result, check the agent type, its `background` field, and whether fork mode prevents waiting in an interactive terminal, VS Code, or a local Desktop session.
quote: With nothing configured, a subagent other than [`web-fetch`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference#web-fetch-subagent) that Claude spawns from your main conversation starts in the background.

claim: The background tool filter for non-fork subagents keeps available MCP tools and limits built-ins to a documented set that includes `ListPlugins`, `ListSkills`, `SearchPlugins`, `SearchSkills`, and `REPL`.
why: Built-ins outside the background set can be removed even when listed in `tools`, and Claude Code reports an error if the list resolves to zero tools.
check: Compare the worker's required tools with the background set, especially for `ListAgents`, which a foreground worker can inherit when cross-session messaging is enabled.
quote: `WebFetch`, `WebSearch`, `TodoWrite`, `Skill`, `ToolSearch`, `EnterWorktree`, `ExitWorktree`, `Monitor`, `TaskStop`, `SendMessage`, `Artifact`, `ListPlugins`, `ListSkills`, `SearchPlugins`, `SearchSkills`, and `REPL`.

claim: Non-fork subagents lose `AskUserQuestion`, `EndConversation`, `EnterPlanMode`, `propose_skills`, `ScheduleWakeup`, `WaitForMcpServers`, and `Workflow` even when listed in `tools`.
why: They also lose `Agent` at the spawn depth limit and `ExitPlanMode` outside plan mode, while forks skip these filters and get a spawning error at the depth limit.
check: Flag a non-fork agent prompt that depends on a filtered tool such as `AskUserQuestion`, `propose_skills`, or `Workflow`.
quote:
* `AskUserQuestion`
* `EndConversation`, which can end only the main conversation; see [EndConversation tool behavior](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference.md#endconversation-tool-behavior)
* `EnterPlanMode`
* `ExitPlanMode`, unless the subagent's [`permissionMode`](#permission-modes) is `plan`
* `propose_skills`
* `ScheduleWakeup`
* `WaitForMcpServers`
* `Workflow`

claim: The `Agent(worker, researcher)` allowlist works for a main-thread agent started with `--agent`, while regular subagents ignore the type list inside the parentheses.
why: A subagent listing `Agent` can spawn any subagent type while depth allows.
check: If an agent must be unable to spawn, check that `Agent` is denied or absent from an explicit `tools` allowlist.
quote: The `Agent(agent_type)` allowlist syntax applies only to an agent running as the main thread with `claude --agent`.

claim: Subagents can by default spawn their own subagents up to three layers below the main conversation; `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH=1` turns nesting off.
why: At the limit the subagent does the work itself and returns one summary.
check: If a worker is intended to be a leaf, check the session depth limit and whether the agent's allowlist or denylist restricts `Agent`.
quote: By default, a subagent can spawn subagents of its own, up to three layers below the main conversation.

claim: By default, an Agent-tool spawn fails with `Concurrent subagent limit reached` when 20 subagents are running in the session, with ultracode sessions exempt.
why: `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS` changes the running limit, and user-started `/subtask` forks and resumes take a slot without being blocked by it.
check: Check Agent-tool fan-out against the effective running limit and occupied slots, since the session has no cumulative cap and workflows and teams have separate limits.
quote: By default, when 20 subagents are running in a session, spawning another with the Agent tool fails with `Concurrent subagent limit reached`

claim: Use a subagent for a side task whose verbose output you will not need again, and define a custom subagent when you repeatedly delegate the same role with the same instructions.
why: The subagent absorbs the verbose work and returns only a summary.
check: Look for side tasks that flood the main context or recurring delegations that repeat the same worker instructions.
quote: Use one when a side task would flood your main conversation with search results, logs, or file contents you won't reference again: the subagent does that work in its own context and returns only the summary. Define a custom subagent when you keep spawning the same kind of worker with the same instructions.

claim: Subagents spend tokens while they work, and their final reports take up context in the main conversation.
why: Many subagents returning detailed results can consume significant main context.
check: Check delegation prompts and agent bodies for a bounded return format (summary, not full dumps).
quote: Running many subagents that each return detailed results can consume significant context, and each subagent spends tokens of its own while it runs.

claim: A fork inherits its parent's conversation history, system prompt, tools, and model, and its shared prompt cache makes it cheaper than a fresh subagent for tasks that need the same context.
why: The fork's first request reuses the parent's prompt cache because its system prompt and tool definitions match the parent's.
check: Where a custom subagent exists only to receive a large pasted context, a fork may be cheaper and simpler.
quote: Because of that reuse, a fork costs less than a fresh subagent for tasks that need the same context.

claim: Set `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL` with `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL_FORCE=1` to use one model for subagents, teammates, and workflow agents, with forks and `model: inherit` skills staying on their parent's model.
why: When the force toggle is on, subagent definitions' `model` fields are ignored and Claude cannot pass a model when launching a subagent.
check: If a setup expects per-agent model selection, check the force toggle and verify the running model in `/tasks`.
quote: Claude Code ignores the `model` field in subagent definitions, and Claude can't pass a model when it starts a subagent.

claim: Subagents inherit the main conversation's extended thinking configuration, and a non-fork subagent's invocation can set `effort` to override its definition's `effort` field.
why: There is no per-subagent thinking setting, `CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL` takes precedence over both effort options, and the invocation parameter requires Claude Code v2.1.292 or later.
check: If a non-fork subagent runs at an unexpected effort, check the invocation, the definition, and `CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL`.
quote: When you ask Claude to run a non-fork subagent at a specific effort level, it can also pass an `effort` parameter for that invocation. The parameter overrides the `effort` field and stays in effect when the subagent is [resumed](#resume-subagents).

claim: Without an `effort` field or parameter, a subagent other than a fork, forked skill, or teammate tries `CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL`, then the spawning subagent's or current turn's effort, then `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_EFFORT`.
why: When none applies, a subagent on the main conversation's model uses the session's selected effort, which does not carry over to a subagent on another model.
check: When a regular subagent has no explicit effort and runs at an unexpected level, check both environment variables, the spawning subagent's effort, and any current-turn override before checking the session's model and effort.
quote:
1. The level in `CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL`, if you set it
2. The `effort` set for the [subagent that spawned it](#let-subagents-spawn-their-own-subagents), or a level set only for the current turn, such as a [skill's `effort`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills#frontmatter-reference)
3. The level in [`CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_EFFORT`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/env-vars#variables)

claim: When subagents share a name, the higher-priority location wins in the order managed settings, `--agents`, project `.claude/agents/`, user `~/.claude/agents/`, plugin.
why: A project agent can shadow a user one, and a managed one overrides both.
check: Look for same-named agents across scopes (including nested project directories, where the closest wins) that hide one another.
quote: When multiple subagents share the same name, Claude Code uses the one from the higher-priority location.

claim: Claude Code loads only one agent when multiple files in the same `.claude/agents/` tree declare the same `name`.
why: The documentation does not specify which file wins within that tree, and `/doctor` reports same-directory name collisions.
check: Look for duplicate `name` values across a single `.claude/agents/` tree and use `/doctor` to help find collisions.
quote: If two files under the same `.claude/agents/` directory declare the same name, Claude Code loads only one of them.

claim: Claude Code skips a project, user, managed, or `--add-dir` subagent file with `name` but no `description`, and records the reason in the debug log.
why: In these scopes, a file without `name` is treated as documentation.
check: For files intended to define agents in these scopes, check the required keys and that the opening `---` is the first line.
quote: **A `name` but no `description`**: Claude Code skips the file and writes the reason to the debug log.

claim: Give each subagent one focused task and a description specific enough for Claude to route work to the intended agent.
why: Claude uses descriptions to decide when to delegate.
check: Check whether descriptions give Claude enough detail to distinguish the intended roles when their responsibilities overlap.
quote: Make each description specific enough to route to the right subagent

claim: Limit each subagent's tool access to only what it needs, for security and focus.
why: Restricting tools improves security and focus, and Bash can still modify files when Edit and Write are excluded.
check: Check whether the agent has more tools than its task needs, including whether a read-only role can still write through Bash.
quote: **Limit tool access:** grant only necessary permissions for security and focus

claim: Use a `PreToolUse` hook when a subagent needs to allow some operations of a tool and block others.
why: The read-only database example validates Bash input and exits with code 2 to block write operations.
check: If a subagent needs Bash for read-only queries, check whether its hook blocks write operations before execution.
quote: For more dynamic control over tool usage, use `PreToolUse` hooks to validate operations before they execute.

claim: Frontmatter hooks of a project subagent are skipped, with only a debug-log error, until the folder containing the agent file is trusted.
why: Trusting a parent folder or launching with `-p` does not itself grant trust to the folder containing the agent definition.
check: For a project agent that depends on frontmatter hooks, verify that the folder containing its file has been trusted, including for CI and `-p`.
quote: Until you trust the folder, the subagent still runs, but Claude Code skips its frontmatter hooks and logs an error to the debug log

claim: Define an MCP server inline in a subagent's `mcpServers` rather than in `.mcp.json` to keep its tool descriptions out of the main conversation.
why: An inline server scoped to the subagent keeps its tool descriptions out of the main context.
check: For a server needed only by one specialist, check whether its global configuration exposes it to the main conversation.
quote: To keep an MCP server out of the main conversation entirely and avoid its tool descriptions consuming context there, define it inline here rather than in `.mcp.json`.

claim: A new subagent invocation creates a fresh instance, so use resume for follow-up work and choose `general-purpose` or a custom subagent when you need a resumable agent ID.
why: Resumed subagents retain their full prior conversation history, and built-in Explore and Plan can finish without providing an agent ID.
check: Check whether follow-up work tries to invoke a fresh instance or depends on Explore or Plan returning an ID.
quote: For work you'll continue later, use `general-purpose` or a custom subagent. The built-in Explore and Plan agents can finish without giving Claude an ID to resume them with.

claim: `isolation: worktree` runs a subagent in a temporary Git worktree based on the repository's default branch by default, and Claude Code can remove the worktree if the agent makes no changes.
why: The worktree gives the subagent a separate checkout whose starting revision and lifetime may differ from the parent session's.
check: Check workers that assume their worktree starts from the parent session's `HEAD` or expect a worktree with no changes to persist.
quote: giving it an isolated copy of the repository. By default, the copy branches from your [default branch](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/worktrees.md#choose-the-base-branch) rather than the parent session's `HEAD`. Claude Code [can remove the worktree](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/worktrees.md#isolate-subagents-with-worktrees) if the subagent makes no changes

claim: With agent teams enabled in an interactive session, an Agent call with a `name` launches a teammate unless it forks or passes `isolation` on the call itself.
why: Claude can name a subagent on its own so it can message the worker later, which can start a team without an explicit request.
check: If ordinary delegations unexpectedly launch teammates, check whether teams are enabled and the Agent call supplies `name`.
quote: Claude launches a teammate when it calls the [Agent tool](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference.md) with a [`name`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents#subagent-names) while agent teams are enabled, unless the call is a [fork](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents.md#fork-the-current-conversation) or passes `isolation` on the call itself.

claim: When a subagent definition is reused as a teammate, its `skills` are not applied, and `mcpServers` apply only to split-pane teammates.
why: Both display modes load skills from project and user settings, while an in-process teammate also uses those settings for MCP instead of the definition's `mcpServers`.
check: Check whether a reused role relies on definition-level `skills` in either display mode or on definition-level `mcpServers` in an in-process teammate.
quote: **`skills`**: Claude Code doesn't apply the definition's `skills` to a teammate in either display mode.

claim: In non-interactive `-p` mode Claude does not spawn teammates, and a subagent Claude names runs as an ordinary subagent even with agent teams enabled.
why: Spawning teammates requires an interactive session.
check: For headless pipelines do not design around teammates.
quote: Claude doesn't spawn teammates, and a subagent that Claude names runs as an ordinary

claim: Use the main conversation rather than a subagent when phases share significant context such as planning, implementation and testing.
why: A non-fork subagent starts fresh and may need time to gather context that the main conversation already has.
check: Check whether separate planning, implementation, and testing agents have to reconstruct significant shared context.
quote: Multiple phases share significant context, such as planning, implementation, and testing

claim: Subagents fit work that is self-contained and can return a summary, produces verbose output, or needs enforced tool restrictions.
why: These are the cases where isolation and restricted tools pay off.
check: An agent whose work needs constant back-and-forth with the user or main context is a poor candidate.
quote: The work is self-contained and can return a summary

claim: Claude Code has five parallel-work mechanisms: subagents, agent view, agent teams, dynamic workflows and projects, differing in who coordinates and whether workers talk to each other.
why: Subagents report to the spawner, agent view sessions report only to the user, teammates message each other, and a workflow script holds the plan.
check: Check that the chosen mechanism matches the work, for example agent teams used where plain subagents would do.
quote: Compare the ways Claude Code can take on multiple tasks at once: subagents, agent view, agent teams, dynamic workflows, and projects.

claim: Running several sessions or subagents at once multiplies token usage.
why: Each worker has its own context and requests.
check: Weigh any parallel design against the plan's usage limits.
quote: Running several sessions or subagents at once multiplies token usage.

claim: Agent teams do not isolate teammates in worktrees, so divide editing work into separate sets of files to avoid conflicts.
why: Two teammates editing the same file leads to overwrites.
check: Check whether multiple teammates are assigned edits to the same files.
quote: Agent teams don't isolate teammates in worktrees, so

claim: Agent teams are experimental, disabled by default, and have known limitations around session resumption, task coordination and shutdown.
why: They need `CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1`.
check: Check whether a team-dependent setup accounts for the documented limits on resumption, task coordination, and shutdown.
quote: Agent teams are experimental and disabled by default.

claim: Compared with one session, agent teams use significantly more tokens and add coordination overhead, and the docs favor a single session or subagents for sequential tasks, same-file edits, or many dependencies.
why: Each teammate is a separate Claude instance with its own context.
check: Flag team use on sequential or tightly coupled work.
quote: For sequential tasks, same-file edits, or work with many dependencies, a single session or

claim: Agent teams are most effective when parallel exploration adds value, as in independent reviews, separately owned modules, competing debugging hypotheses, or cross-layer work with separate owners.
why: These uses let teammates explore independently, own separate work, or compare findings.
check: Check whether the proposed teammates can work independently or test competing ideas in parallel.
quote: Agent teams are most effective for tasks where parallel exploration adds real value.

claim: For most workflows, start an agent team with 3-5 teammates and scale up only when more teammates can work simultaneously.
why: Token cost scales linearly and coordination overhead rises with team size.
check: Review larger teams for work that benefits from the additional simultaneous effort.
quote: Start with 3-5 teammates for most workflows.

claim: Teammates load CLAUDE.md, MCP servers and skills like a regular session but do not inherit the lead's conversation history, so spawn prompts must carry task-specific context.
why: The spawn prompt is how the lead passes task-specific context from its own conversation.
check: Check spawn prompts for the objective, scope and constraints.
quote: Teammates load project context automatically, including CLAUDE.md, MCP servers, and skills, but they don't inherit the lead's conversation history.

claim: A teammate's permission mode cannot be set at spawn, and it starts in the lead's mode unless the lead uses `dontAsk`, in which case it starts in Manual mode.
why: This inheritance includes `bypassPermissions` when the lead uses `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, and the docs give version requirements for split-pane teammates of Manual and `dontAsk` leads.
check: Check whether the team expects an independent spawn-time mode or assumes a `dontAsk` lead passes that mode to its teammates.
quote: You can't set per-teammate permission modes at spawn time.

claim: There are no nested teams and the lead is fixed for the session's lifetime.
why: Only the lead manages the team, and one team exists per session.
check: Do not design hierarchical team structures.
quote: teammates cannot spawn their own teammates. Only the lead can manage the team.

claim: New users of agent teams should start with research or review tasks that have clear boundaries and need no code writing.
why: They show the value of parallel exploration without the coordination problems of parallel implementation.
check: Be wary of teams whose first use is parallel code edits.
quote: start with tasks that have clear boundaries and don't require writing code: reviewing a PR, researching a library, or investigating a bug.

claim: A dynamic workflow script holds the loop, branching, and intermediate results, so the main conversation's context receives only the final answer.
why: With subagents, skills and teams Claude is the orchestrator and every result enters a context window.
check: For fan-outs over dozens of items, check whether a workflow would spare the main context.
quote: A workflow script holds the loop, the branching, and the intermediate results itself, so Claude's context holds only the final answer.

claim: Workflows can raise result quality through a repeatable pattern, such as independent agents adversarially reviewing each other's findings or drafting a plan from several angles.
why: The docs describe cross-checking findings or weighing draft plans as ways to improve on a single pass.
check: For work that needs cross-verification, check whether the workflow has independent agents review findings or compare alternative plans.
quote: it can have independent agents adversarially review each other's findings before they're reported

claim: A workflow run can use meaningfully more tokens than doing the same task in conversation.
why: Many agents are spawned; the docs advise running a small slice first and watching per-agent token use in `/workflows`.
check: For a large workflow, check whether a small trial and the per-agent token counts in `/workflows` were used to gauge cost.
quote: A workflow spawns many agents, so a single run can use meaningfully more tokens than working through the same task in conversation.

claim: A dynamic workflow allows up to 1,000 agents per run, up to 16 concurrent agents by default, and up to 4,096 items per `parallel()` or `pipeline()` call.
why: Available CPUs can lower default concurrency, and `CLAUDE_CODE_WORKFLOW_MAX_CONCURRENT_AGENTS` can set the concurrency limit on supported versions.
check: Check scripts against the run and call caps and the concurrency limit effective in the launch environment.
quote:
Up to 4,096 items in a single `parallel()` or `pipeline()` call: the runtime rejects a longer list with an error | A silent cap would drop part of the workload without telling the script |
| 1,000 agents total per run

claim: The workflow size guideline defaults to `medium` (fewer than 10 agents), or `small` (fewer than 5) when signed in on Pro with Claude Code v2.1.271 or later.
why: A prompt calling for a different scale overrides it.
check: Check whether a setup treats `workflowSizeGuideline` as an enforced cap even though a prompt can override it.
quote: The default is `medium`, or `small` when you're signed in on a Pro plan with Claude Code v2.1.271 or later.

claim: With ultracode on, Claude plans a workflow for each substantive task, which increases request token use and can reach subscription usage limits sooner.
why: Ultracode also suppresses the Large workflow warning and the concurrency limit for subagents Claude spawns through the Agent tool.
check: For routine work, check whether persistent `ultracode` settings enable automatic workflows and assess their token use.
quote: This applies to every task in the session, so each request uses more tokens and takes longer than the same request without a workflow.

claim: The `ultracode` keyword does not opt a prompt into a workflow through `-p`, unstamped SDK input, scheduled tasks, webhooks, or relayed pull request comments.
why: An Agent SDK app can opt in with keyboard input marked `{ kind: "human" }`.
check: Check that automation does not depend on the keyword to initiate a workflow from one of the unsupported inputs.
quote: It doesn't start a workflow when it reaches the session another way:

claim: Workflow agents follow the subagent model order, with the session model as fallback and a substitute when an `availableModels` allowlist blocks the script's choice.
why: The model named for a stage counts as the per-invocation choice, and blocked requests follow the subagent model substitution rules.
check: Compare each stage's intended model with its configured model and any `availableModels` allowlist, especially when the stage depends on a specific model.
quote: A model the script names for a stage counts as the per-invocation model in that order.

claim: In `-p` and the Agent SDK, workflow launches go through normal Workflow-tool permission evaluation without the interactive workflow confirmation prompt.
why: An allow rule, auto mode, bypass mode, a hook, or host approval can authorize the launch, with `PreToolUse` hook approval alone insufficient in plan mode.
check: Check which permission path the headless run uses to authorize the Workflow call.
quote: In `claude -p` and the Agent SDK, the Workflow tool call goes through the same [permission evaluation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/permissions.md#how-permissions-are-evaluated) as the rest of the session. Deny rules, ask rules, and `dontAsk` mode apply to the call.

claim: Anthropic recommends `--bare` for scripts and SDK calls to skip normal auto-discovery of hooks, skills, commands, subagents, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory, and CLAUDE.md.
why: Bare mode reduces startup time, still reads settings and permission rules, and loads skills from directories supplied with `--add-dir`.
check: Check whether scripted runs depend on hooks that bare mode skips or assume `--bare` bypasses permission rules in settings files.
quote: `--bare` is the recommended mode for scripted and SDK calls, and will become the default for `-p` in a future release.

claim: In Claude Code v2.1.286 and later, bare mode disables background commands and background subagents.
why: The limits tied to `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_BACKGROUND_TASKS` apply.
check: Do not combine `--bare` with designs that depend on background subagents.
quote: Claude can't run background commands or background subagents

claim: After the turn ends and stdin closes, `claude -p` stops waiting for background work and drops partial results after 10 idle minutes by default, except while a background command from the main conversation runs.
why: `CLAUDE_CODE_PRINT_BG_WAIT_CEILING_MS` changes the ceiling, with `0` disabling it.
check: Check whether a headless run needs to keep background subagents or workflows alive longer than its configured idle ceiling.
quote: Claude Code stops whatever is still running after 10 minutes of continuous idle waiting by default and drops its partial result.

claim: For unattended runs, use `--permission-prompts none` to skip the permission host, deny unresolved prompts, and tell Claude to stop retrying denied requests.
why: Permission rules, `PermissionRequest` hooks, and the selected permission mode still apply before Claude Code denies an unresolved request.
check: Check whether an unattended run with a permission host can wait for approvals that nobody is available to answer.
quote: Pass `--permission-prompts none` when nobody is available to answer permission prompts, for example in a scheduled job.

claim: `/goal` sends the condition and conversation to the configured small fast model, which judges completion from the transcript without running commands or reading files.
why: The evaluator can judge only what Claude has surfaced in the conversation.
check: Check that goal conditions name a measurable end state and a check whose output appears in the transcript.
quote: It doesn't run commands or read files independently, so write the condition as something Claude's own output can demonstrate.

claim: To bound a `/goal` run, include a turn or time clause in the completion condition.
why: Claude reports progress against the clause each turn, and the evaluator judges it from the conversation.
check: Check open-ended goals for a turn or time clause when the run needs a bound.
quote: To bound how long a goal runs, include a turn or time clause in the condition

claim: If a subagent or background shell command is still running when a turn ends, `/goal` skips evaluation for that turn.
why: After 30 minutes of waiting by default a check-in becomes due, and a completed background task delivers its result as a new turn.
check: Check for running subagents or shell commands when a goal has no end-of-turn verdict.
quote: If a subagent or a background shell command is still running when a turn ends, Claude Code skips the evaluation for that turn.

claim: Session-scoped recurring tasks fire only while Claude Code is running and idle and expire 30 days after creation, with a 7-day limit for `CronCreate` tasks created on versions before v2.1.330.
why: An expiring recurring task fires one final time and deletes itself, and a backgrounded session can keep its `/loop` tasks running.
check: Check whether recurring work needs to survive its session or expiry, and check the creation version for existing `CronCreate` tasks.
quote: Recurring tasks automatically expire 30 days after creation. The task fires one final time, then deletes itself. This bounds how long a forgotten loop can run. Before v2.1.330, the limit was 7 days, and recurring tasks created with `CronCreate` on those versions keep it.

claim: Use cloud scheduled tasks for work that must run without your machine, Desktop tasks for local files and tools, and `/loop` for quick polling in a session.
why: Cloud tasks run without your machine, Desktop tasks use your machine without requiring an open session, and `/loop` needs an open session.
check: Match each scheduled job to the right tier.
quote: Use **cloud tasks** for work that should run reliably without your machine.

claim: When Monitor is available and a script can stream the event, it avoids polling and is often more token-efficient than rerunning a prompt on an interval.
why: Monitor runs a background script and streams its output line by line into the session.
check: For dynamic `/loop` polling, check whether an available Monitor watch can report the relevant event directly.
quote: which avoids polling altogether and is often more token-efficient and responsive than re-running a prompt on an interval.

claim: For LLM applications, start with the simplest solution and add complexity only as needed, since optimizing a single LLM call is often enough.
why: Agentic systems often trade latency and cost for better task performance.
check: Check whether a multi-agent design needs the added complexity for its task.
quote: When building applications with LLMs, we recommend finding the simplest solution possible, and only increasing complexity when needed.

claim: Orchestrator-workers suits complex tasks with unpredictable subtasks, while parallelization suits independent subtasks or multiple attempts for higher confidence.
why: The orchestrator decides subtasks from the input, unlike fixed parallel sectioning.
check: Match the delegation pattern to whether the subtasks are known beforehand.
quote: complex tasks where you can’t predict the subtasks needed

claim: An evaluator-optimizer loop fits tasks with clear evaluation criteria where iterative refinement provides measurable value.
why: A good fit is a response a human can demonstrably improve with feedback and for which the LLM can give that kind of feedback.
check: Check whether a reviewer-fixer loop has clear evaluation criteria and feedback that demonstrably improves the output.
quote: The two signs of good fit are, first, that LLM responses can be demonstrably improved when a human articulates their feedback; and second, that the LLM can provide such feedback.

claim: Anthropic gives routing easy or common queries to a smaller, cost-efficient model and hard or unusual queries to a stronger model as an example of optimizing performance.
why: The examples are Claude Haiku 4.5 and Claude Sonnet 4.5, and the pattern fits distinct categories that can be classified accurately.
check: Where workload categories can be classified accurately, check whether easy and hard queries benefit from different model assignments.
quote: Routing easy/common questions to smaller, cost-efficient models like Claude Haiku 4.5 and hard/unusual questions to more capable models like Claude Sonnet 4.5 to optimize for best performance.

claim: Anthropic notes that much of the tooling landscape described in its Building Effective Agents post has changed since December 2024.
why: The note qualifies the post's tooling descriptions.
check: If an audit relies on a specific tool detail from the post, check that the detail still applies to the setup.
quote: Note: Much of the tooling landscape described in this post has changed since December 2024.

claim: Anthropic's research data showed typical token use of about 4× chat for agents and about 15× chat for multi-agent systems, making task value important to economic viability.
why: In Anthropic's BrowseComp analysis, token usage alone accounted for 80% of performance variance.
check: Assess whether the task value justifies the extra token spend, using the reported figures as a research comparison.
quote: In our data, agents typically use about 4× more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats.

claim: Anthropic found multi-agent Research effective for valuable work with heavy parallelism, information beyond one context window, and numerous complex tools.
why: Breadth-first research offers independent search paths, while domains that require shared context or have many inter-agent dependencies can be poor fits for multi-agent systems.
check: Check whether the task offers independent work or instead needs shared context or frequent coordination between agents.
quote: We’ve found that multi-agent systems excel at valuable tasks that involve heavy parallelization, information that exceeds single context windows, and interfacing with numerous complex tools.

claim: Anthropic's Research post says most coding tasks have fewer truly parallelizable parts than research and that agents struggle with real-time coordination and delegation.
why: The post identifies domains with shared context or many dependencies as a poor fit for multi-agent systems.
check: Before recommending coding fan-out, check which subtasks can proceed independently.
quote: most coding tasks involve fewer truly parallelizable tasks than research, and LLM agents are not yet great at coordinating and delegating to other agents in real time.

claim: A delegation brief to a worker should give an objective, an output format, guidance on tools and sources, and clear task boundaries.
why: Without detail, subagents duplicate work, leave gaps or misread the task.
check: Look at the delegation instructions in agent bodies and the lead's prompts for these four elements.
quote: Each subagent needs an objective, an output format, guidance on the tools and sources to use, and clear task boundaries.

claim: In Anthropic's Research prototype, short, vague delegation prompts often led subagents to misinterpret the task or repeat each other's searches.
why: In one semiconductor-shortage example, one subagent researched the 2021 automotive chip crisis while two others duplicated work on 2025 supply chains.
check: Check for vague delegation prompts that leave research boundaries or the division of work unclear.
quote: Without detailed task descriptions, agents duplicate work, leave gaps, or fail to find necessary information.

claim: Anthropic's Research lead prompts scale effort by complexity, from 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls for a simple lookup to potentially more than 10 subagents for complex research.
why: Early Research agents overinvested in simple queries, sometimes spawning 50 subagents.
check: Check whether the research lead scales effort to the task, using 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each for direct comparisons as one example from the post.
quote: Simple fact-finding requires just 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls, direct comparisons might need 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each, and complex research might use more than 10 subagents with clearly divided responsibilities.

claim: Give each tool a distinct purpose and a clear description, since bad descriptions can send agents down the wrong path.
why: With many MCP tools, agents meet unseen tools of widely varying description quality.
check: Look for tools with unclear or overlapping purposes or descriptions that could lead an agent to choose the wrong tool.
quote: Bad tool descriptions can send agents down completely wrong paths, so each tool needs a distinct purpose and a clear description.

claim: For suitable outputs, let subagents store artifacts independently and send the coordinator lightweight references to reduce information loss and token overhead.
why: Routing large outputs through the lead causes a game of telephone.
check: Check whether large structured outputs, such as code or reports, are copied through the coordinator when a reference would suffice.
quote: Subagents call tools to store their work in external systems, then pass lightweight references back to the coordinator.

claim: In the Research system described by Anthropic, the lead waited for each batch of subagents to finish, which prevented it from steering them and kept them from coordinating.
why: The post expected asynchronous execution to pay off as models improve.
check: In a similarly synchronous research design, check whether waiting for a whole batch blocks steering or progress.
quote: Currently, our lead agents execute subagents synchronously, waiting for each set of subagents to complete before proceeding.

claim: For complex Research queries, Anthropic cut research time by up to 90% by launching 3-5 subagents in parallel and having the subagents use 3 or more tools in parallel.
why: Sequential searches had been slow in the earlier Research system.
check: Check whether a complex research workflow runs independent searches serially even though they can run concurrently.
quote: the lead agent spins up 3-5 subagents in parallel rather than serially; (2) the subagents use 3+ tools in parallel. These changes cut research time by up to 90% for complex queries

claim: Prompt multi-agent research systems with a framework for collaboration that defines the division of labor, problem-solving approaches, and effort budgets.
why: Small changes to the lead prompt can unpredictably change how subagents behave.
check: Check whether the lead prompt provides those collaboration details and whether evaluations exercise interactions between agents.
quote: Multi-agent systems have emergent behaviors, which arise without specific programming.

claim: In Anthropic's long-running web app harness, an initializer sets up the environment, feature list, and progress file, and later coding sessions work on one feature at a time.
why: The harness addressed attempts to build everything in one go or declare the app complete too early, and later sessions were asked to leave the project in a clean state.
check: For analogous multi-session coding work, check whether each new session can recover progress, pick one unfinished feature, and leave the project in a clean state.
quote: the next iteration of the coding agent was then asked to work on only one feature at a time.

claim: Anthropic used JSON for the long-running coding harness's feature checklist after observing fewer inappropriate edits than with Markdown.
why: The coding agent was prompted to edit only the `passes` field and to leave the feature requirements and tests intact.
check: Check whether a long-running coding harness preserves checklist requirements while still allowing status updates.
quote: the model is less likely to inappropriately change or overwrite JSON files compared to Markdown files.

claim: In Anthropic's long-running web app harness, Claude mostly did well at verifying features end to end after being explicitly prompted to test as a user with browser automation.
why: Without explicit prompting, Claude tended to miss end-to-end failures even when it ran unit tests or curl checks.
check: Check whether a comparable web app harness requires user-level verification before a feature is marked complete.
quote: Claude mostly did well at verifying features end-to-end once explicitly prompted to use browser automation tools and do all testing as a human user would.

claim: Anthropic called it an open question whether one general coding agent or specialized agents (testing, QA, cleanup) perform better.
why: The post's initializer and coding sessions differed in their initial user prompt, and the harness was optimized for full-stack web app development.
check: Check whether a comparable coding harness has evaluated the benefits of specialized testing, QA, or cleanup roles.
quote: it’s still unclear whether a single, general-purpose coding agent performs best across contexts, or if better performance can be achieved through a multi-agent architecture

claim: To use a cheaper model for an API subtask while preserving the main loop's prompt cache, run the subtask in a subagent and keep the main loop on one model.
why: Switching the main loop's model mid-session invalidates its cache, and Managed Agents can use a `multiagent` roster entry for the subtask.
check: Check whether a cost-driven switch changes the main loop's model when the setup depends on preserving its cached prefix.
quote: Spawn a **subagent** with the cheaper model for the sub-task; keep the main loop on one model.

claim: Agent files can set `color` and `experimental.cacheTtl`, while `--agents` JSON ignores `color` and `experimental`.
why: The frontmatter reference documents display color and an experimental prompt-cache lifetime for file-based agents.
check: If a setup depends on either option, check whether it is defined in an agent file or passed as `--agents` JSON.
quote: **Ignored fields**: `color` and `experimental` aren't accepted here and are ignored rather than rejected.

claim: A non-fork subagent gets a startup roster of `main` and other named agents only if it has `SendMessage` and at least one other agent is named.
why: Claude Code takes the roster when the subagent starts, so it omits agents named later.
check: Check whether a worker assumes the startup roster is available or includes agents named after it started.
quote: The roster appears only when the subagent's tools include `SendMessage` and at least one other agent has a name, whether Claude named it when spawning it or it runs as an [agent team](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-teams.md) teammate. It is a snapshot taken when the subagent starts, so agents named later don't appear.

claim: A fork cannot spawn further forks.
why: A design that needs a second layer of forks cannot use the first fork to launch it.
check: Check whether a delegated fork is expected to launch another fork.
quote: A fork can't spawn further forks.

claim: If an agent-team lead creates too few tasks, ask for smaller pieces, with 5-6 tasks per teammate as the documented guideline.
why: This keeps teammates productive and lets the lead reassign work if someone gets stuck.
check: If there are too few tasks for teammates to work independently, check whether the lead can break the work into more self-contained deliverables.
quote: If it isn't creating enough tasks, ask it to split the work into smaller pieces. Having 5-6 tasks per teammate keeps everyone productive and lets the lead reassign work if someone gets stuck.

claim: By default, a workflow shows a Large workflow warning above 25 scheduled agents or 1.5 million projected tokens, with ultracode sessions exempt.
why: The warning is advisory, and an explicitly selected size guideline replaces the default agent-count threshold.
check: Check whether a setup expects the warning to cap or pause a run, or relies on the default threshold despite custom size settings or ultracode.
quote: When a workflow schedules more than 25 agents, or its projected token total passes 1.5 million, its progress line in the task panel below the input box shows a `Large workflow` warning.

claim: `/goal` evaluation tokens are billed in addition to main-turn spend.
why: The session's configured provider runs a separate evaluator that judges the transcript without tool calls.
check: Include `/goal` evaluator tokens alongside the main turns when auditing the total cost of a goal run.
quote: Evaluation tokens are billed in addition to main-turn spend.

claim: In Anthropic's internal research eval, an Opus 4 lead with Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Opus 4 by 90.2%.
why: The post describes breadth-first research queries that can be decomposed into independent search directions as a strong use case.
check: Check that comparisons citing the 90.2% gain retain the internal research eval and model setup.
quote: We found that a multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on our internal research eval.
